stem: A security steering committee has approved an acceptable use policy, but eight months later an audit finds three business units still running their own conflicting versions. The committee meets quarterly and has no standing agenda item for policy status. Which governance element is missing?
options: A defined policy review and exception process with named owners
A more detailed acceptable use policy with additional prohibited activities
Mandatory annual security awareness training for all three business units
A centralized SIEM to detect violations of the acceptable use policy
explanation: Governance fails here at the maintenance layer, not the authoring layer. A policy needs an owner, a review cadence, and a documented exception path; without those, local variants appear and nobody is accountable for reconciling them. Adding more prohibited activities makes a longer document that is still unmaintained. Awareness training tells staff what the policy says but does not resolve three competing authoritative versions. A SIEM detects technical violations after the fact and has no visibility into which written policy a unit believes it is following.

stem: A risk register lists a legacy application with an annualized loss expectancy of $180,000. A proposed replacement costs $450,000 up front and reduces the ALE to $15,000. Leadership must justify the spend over a three-year horizon. What is the most defensible analysis?
options: Compare $495,000 in three-year residual loss plus project cost against $540,000 in retained risk
Accept the risk, because the replacement cost exceeds the single-year annualized loss expectancy
Transfer the risk to a cyber insurance policy, since the premium will be lower than $450,000
Apply compensating controls only, because any quantitative estimate of ALE is inherently unreliable
explanation: Quantitative risk decisions compare total cost of the treatment against total retained risk over the same period. Three years of the current ALE is $540,000; the replacement costs $450,000 plus $45,000 of residual loss, so $495,000 — the treatment is justified. Comparing a capital cost to a single year's ALE is the classic error and would reject nearly every multi-year control. Insurance transfers financial impact but not the operational or regulatory consequences, and the premium is not the only cost. Dismissing ALE because it is an estimate discards the only common unit leadership and security share.

stem: A payroll processor will receive employee bank details and tax identifiers. Procurement has a signed master services agreement and a current SOC 2 Type II report. The security team is asked what else is required before data flows. What is the most important remaining item?
options: A data processing agreement defining permitted use, breach notification timelines, and return or destruction at termination
A penetration test of the vendor's production environment performed by your own red team
A copy of the vendor's cyber insurance certificate naming your organization
Evidence that the vendor encrypts data at rest using AES-256 specifically
explanation: A SOC 2 Type II attests that controls operated effectively during a window; it does not constrain what the vendor may do with your data, when they must tell you about a breach, or what happens at exit. Those obligations live in a data processing agreement, and without one you have assurance about their controls but no rights over your data. Your own red team testing a third party's production environment is rarely contractually permitted and duplicates the audit. An insurance certificate addresses recovery of loss, not prevention or notification. A specific cipher is a control detail the SOC 2 scope already covers.

stem: An organization operates in the EU and California. A customer submits a request to delete all personal data. Marketing objects that the record is needed to suppress future mailings to that person. How should the compliance requirement be satisfied?
options: Retain a minimal suppression record under the legal obligation basis and delete all other personal data
Deny the deletion request, because a suppression list is a legitimate business interest
Delete every record including the suppression entry, then rely on the customer to re-opt out
Anonymize the entire customer record and retain it in full for marketing analytics
explanation: Both GDPR and CCPA allow retaining the minimum data needed to honor the request itself — a suppression or do-not-contact entry — while erasing everything else. That is data minimization applied to the exception, not an exception to it. Denying the request outright misstates legitimate interest, which does not override an erasure right for marketing data. Deleting the suppression entry means the person starts receiving mail again, converting a satisfied request into a fresh violation. Retaining a full record and calling it anonymized fails, because data that can still be linked to an individual is pseudonymized, not anonymous.

stem: An internal audit and an external penetration test are both scheduled for the same quarter on the same payment application. A manager proposes cancelling one to save budget. What distinction should the security lead present?
options: The audit verifies whether controls exist and operate as documented; the test verifies whether they can be defeated
The audit is required by regulation while the penetration test is a discretionary best practice
The audit examines technical configuration while the penetration test reviews policy and procedure
The audit is performed by an independent party while the penetration test is performed internally
explanation: They answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other. An audit samples evidence to confirm a control is designed and operating as written; a penetration test attempts to defeat controls in practice and regularly finds gaps that pass audit — a documented, operating patch process that still leaves an unauthenticated remote code execution exposed. Regulatory obligation varies by framework and often covers both. The option assigning technical configuration to the audit and policy review to the test inverts their scopes. Independence is a property either engagement can have; audits are frequently internal and penetration tests frequently external.

stem: Simulated phishing click rates dropped from 18% to 4% over a year, but the reporting rate stayed flat at 6% and the mean time to report is 90 minutes. What does this pattern most likely indicate about the awareness program?
options: Users are avoiding the lure but have not been taught that reporting is the expected action
The simulation difficulty has been set too low and no longer reflects real phishing
Technical email filtering improved, so the awareness program had no measurable effect
Users are reporting to their managers instead of to the security team, so the metric is wrong
explanation: Not clicking and reporting are separate behaviors requiring separate reinforcement. A falling click rate with a flat reporting rate is the signature of a program that trained avoidance but never made reporting easy, expected, or rewarded — and the 90-minute mean time confirms it is not reflexive. Undetected campaigns are exactly the ones where a fast report is the only early signal. Lower simulation difficulty would depress click rates but would not hold reporting flat. Filtering improvements do not reach simulations, which are injected past the gateway. Manager-relay is possible but would still eventually surface, not flatline for a year.

stem: During a risk assessment, a business owner states that a control gap is acceptable because the affected system will be decommissioned in eighteen months. What is the correct treatment of this decision?
options: Record a formal risk acceptance with an owner, expiry date, and review trigger if the timeline slips
Close the finding, since a planned decommission removes the risk from the register
Escalate immediately to the board, because risk acceptance is never delegable to a business owner
Reclassify the risk as transferred, since the decommission project now owns the outcome
explanation: Risk acceptance is a legitimate treatment, but it is only defensible when documented with a named accountable owner, an explicit expiry, and a trigger to revisit if the assumption changes. Decommission dates slip constantly, and an undated acceptance quietly becomes permanent. Closing the finding erases the exposure that still exists for eighteen months. Board escalation depends on whether the residual risk exceeds the defined tolerance; routing every acceptance upward destroys the point of a tolerance threshold. Transfer means shifting financial or legal impact to another party, such as insurance, not reassigning it to an internal project.

stem: An organization is drafting documentation that states all remote access must use multifactor authentication, without specifying products or configuration steps. Which document type is being written?
options: A policy
A procedure
A standard
A guideline
explanation: A policy states mandatory intent at a high level — what must be true — without binding the organization to a specific implementation. A standard would name the accepted technology or configuration, such as which authenticator types are approved. A procedure would give the ordered steps an administrator follows to enrol a user. A guideline is advisory rather than mandatory, and the word 'must' rules it out. Keeping these separate is what lets you change vendors without reopening the policy.

stem: A software supplier is acquired by a company headquartered in a jurisdiction subject to export restrictions relevant to your industry. The contract has two years remaining and the software is embedded in a production line. What should happen first?
options: Re-run third-party due diligence against the new ownership and assess the change-of-control terms
Invoke the termination clause immediately to eliminate the jurisdictional exposure
Continue as normal, because the contract was signed with the original entity and remains binding
Replace the software with an in-house build before the next release cycle
explanation: Change of ownership resets the risk profile — jurisdiction, sub-processors, data location, and support obligations can all move — so the first step is to reassess against the new owner and read what the change-of-control clause actually entitles you to. Terminating immediately without that assessment risks halting a production line over an exposure that may be manageable, and may not even be contractually available. Assuming the original contract insulates you misunderstands acquisition: obligations transfer to the acquirer along with the risk. Building a replacement is a possible outcome of the assessment, not a first move.

stem: A quarterly compliance report shows 100% of servers passing the hardening baseline. A security engineer notes the scan only covers systems registered in the configuration management database, and roughly 15% of production hosts were built by a team that does not register them. How should the reported metric be characterized?
options: The metric measures compliance of known assets and overstates coverage because asset inventory is incomplete
The metric is accurate, since unregistered hosts fall outside the defined compliance scope
The metric is invalid and should be replaced with a count of vulnerabilities found
The metric is acceptable if the 15% are non-production or low-criticality systems
explanation: A compliance percentage is only as trustworthy as the denominator. Reporting 100% while 15% of production is invisible to the scanner presents an assurance level the organization does not have, and asset inventory is the control that fails first. Declaring unregistered hosts out of scope makes the metric true by definition and useless in practice — it rewards not registering. Swapping in a vulnerability count measures something different and inherits the same blind spot. The stem states these are production hosts, so the criticality escape does not apply.
